lessons.title: Setting up your block moulds: wooden vs. metal moulds
lessons.body: Before you make blocks, you need a mould. You can buy one or make it yourself. The two main types are wooden and metal. Wooden moulds are cheaper and easier to make if you have basic carpentry skills. Use hardwood like mahogany or iroko, not softwood like pine, because softwood warps when wet. A standard wooden mould for a 6-inch block (15 cm x 20 cm x 40 cm) costs about $20â$30 in materials. But wooden moulds wear out fasterâafter 200â300 blocks, the edges round off and blocks become uneven. Metal moulds, usually made from 2â3 mm steel sheet, cost $50â$100 but last for thousands of blocks. They keep their shape better, so your blocks are more uniform. If you plan to sell blocks, invest in metal. For a small backyard project, wood is fine. When setting up, make sure the mould is square: measure diagonalsâthey must be equal. Bolt or screw all joints tightly. Any gap larger than 1 mm will let mortar leak and create weak edges. For mass production, build a mould that makes 2 or 3 blocks at once. A 3-block metal mould can cost $150 but triples your output. Set the mould on a flat, level surfaceâa wooden pallet or concrete slab. If the ground is uneven, blocks will be different thicknesses. Also, decide if you want a bottom plate or if you will cast on the ground. A bottom plate makes moving easier but adds cost. In Africa, many artisans use a simple wooden mould with a removable base. Whatever you choose, keep the mould clean and oiled (next lesson). Check for wear weekly. Replace or repair any bent sides. A good mould is the backbone of block making.

lessons.title: Preparing the mould: oiling and cleaning for easy release
lessons.body: If you skip oiling, your blocks will stick, and you will break corners trying to remove them. Oil creates a thin barrier so the concrete does not bond to the mould. Use any light oil: used engine oil, palm oil, or commercial release agent. Used engine oil is cheap and works well, but it stains the blocks dark. If you want clean-looking blocks, use vegetable oil or a proper mould oil. Apply oil with a rag or brush. Coat all inside surfaces, especially corners and edges. Do not pour oilâjust a thin film. Too much oil can cause surface bubbles. Clean the mould after every use. Scrape off stuck concrete with a wooden scraper or wire brush. Do not use a metal hammerâit dents the mould. Rinse with water and dry. Then oil again before the next block. If you are making many blocks, oil the mould every 5â10 blocks, or whenever you see the mix starting to stick. In hot, dry weather, oil evaporates faster, so oil more often. For wooden moulds, oil also protects the wood from water damage. But do not soak the woodâtoo much oil can soften it. A good routine: after demoulding, clean the mould immediately while concrete is still green (soft). Then oil it and set it aside for the next batch. If you are using a manual machine, follow the manufacturer's instructionsâsome machines need grease on moving parts, not oil on the mould faces. Keep a small bucket of oil and a rag near your work area. A dirty, rusty mould will ruin your blocks. In Africa, where dust and sand are common, cover your moulds when not in use to keep them clean. Proper preparation takes 2 minutes per mould but saves hours of frustration.

lessons.title: Filling and compacting the mix for solid blocks
lessons.body: Filling and compacting is where strength is made or lost. Your mix should be stiffâlike damp sand that holds its shape when squeezed. A typical mix for solid blocks is 1 part cement to 6 parts sand (by volume) for a 6-inch block. For stronger blocks, use 1:5. Add water gradually; too much water weakens the block. A good test: squeeze a handfulâit should form a ball that does not crumble or drip water. Now fill the mould. Use a shovel or trowel to place the mix in layers. For a 6-inch block, fill halfway (about 10 cm deep), then compact. Compaction removes air pockets. Use a wooden tamper or a steel rod. Tamp evenly across the surfaceâabout 20â25 strokes per layer. Do not just poke; lift the tamper and drop it. For the second layer, fill to the top of the mould and tamp again. Overfill slightly (1â2 cm) because the mix will settle. Then strike off the excess with a straight edge (a piece of wood or steel). Move the straight edge in a sawing motion across the top. Do not press down hardâjust level it. For hollow blocks, you will use a core (a metal or wooden insert) to create voids. But for solid blocks, you want a dense, uniform fill. If you see voids or honeycomb after demoulding, you did not compact enough. In Africa, many makers use a manual vibration method: tap the sides of the mould with a hammer or lift the mould 2â3 cm and drop it on the ground 10 times. This settles the mix. But be carefulâtoo much dropping can cause segregation. After filling and compacting, let the block sit for 10â15 minutes before moving. This allows initial set. Then demould (next lesson). Remember: a well-compacted block is 30% stronger than a poorly compacted one. Take your time.

lessons.title: Using a manual block-making machine vs. hand tamping
lessons.body: You have two main options for compacting: a manual block-making machine or hand tamping. A manual machine (like a CINVA-Ram or a local copy) uses a lever to compress the mix. It costs $200â$500 but produces denser, stronger blocks and is faster. With a machine, you fill the mould, pull the lever, and the block is compressed with high pressure. You can make 200â400 blocks per day with a team. Hand tamping uses a wooden or metal tamper to compact the mix manually. It is cheap (a tamper costs $5) but slowerâmaybe 50â100 blocks per day. Hand tamping also gives less consistent density; some blocks will be stronger than others. If you are building a house for yourself, hand tamping is fine. If you are selling blocks, a machine pays for itself in a few months. But machines need maintenance: grease the moving parts, check the lever, and replace worn parts. In rural Africa, where spare parts are hard to find, a simple wooden tamper is more reliable. You can also make a simple vibrating table from a small motor and a metal plate. That costs $100â$200 and works well for small production. The key difference is pressure. A manual machine applies 2â5 MPa (megapascals) of pressure; hand tamping gives maybe 0.5â1 MPa. Higher pressure means you can use less cement (1:7 mix instead of 1:6) and still get strong blocks. But for beginners, start with hand tamping to learn the feel of the mix. Then upgrade to a machine when you have consistent sales. Whichever you choose, the goal is a dense block with no voids. Test your blocks: drop one from waist height onto a hard surface. If it shatters, your compaction or mix is wrong. If it stays intact, you are doing well.

lessons.title: Removing blocks from moulds without breaking corners
lessons.body: Removing blocks too early or roughly is the number one cause of broken corners. Wait until the block is firm enough to hold its shape but still soft enough to release easily. This is usually 10â30 minutes after compaction, depending on weather. In hot, dry weather, it might be 10 minutes; in cool, humid weather, 30 minutes. Test by pressing the top of the block with your thumb. If it leaves a slight dent but does not crumble, it is ready. To remove, first loosen the mould. For a wooden mould, tap the sides gently with a rubber mallet or a block of wood. Do not use a metal hammerâit will crack the wood. For a metal mould, you may have a release mechanism (a lever or a screw). If not, tap the sides. Then lift the mould straight up. Do not twist or tiltâthat breaks corners. If the block sticks, do not force it. Wait 5 more minutes and try again. If it still sticks, your oiling was insufficient. Next time, oil more. For a bottomless mould (casting on the ground), you lift the mould off the block. For a mould with a bottom plate, you flip the whole thing over onto a pallet or board, then lift the mould. Always lift the mould, not the block. After demoulding, leave the block on a flat pallet in the shade for 24 hours. Do not move it. Then cure it by watering it twice a day for 7 days. Broken corners mean wasted cement and time. A good demoulder can remove 200 blocks per day with less than 5% breakage. In Africa, many use a simple wooden mould with a removable base. Practice on a few blocks first. If you break one, remix itâdo not throw it away. With practice, you will get a feel for the right time.

lessons.title: Making special blocks: hollow, solid, and interlocking types
lessons.body: Once you master solid blocks, you can make special types that save cement, reduce weight, or speed up construction. Hollow blocks have two or three vertical voids. They use 30â40% less cement and are lighter, so they are easier to carry. To make them, you need a mould with coresâmetal or wooden inserts that create the holes. Fill the mould around the cores, compact, and remove the cores after demoulding. A standard hollow block (6-inch) has two voids, each about 10 cm x 15 cm. The wall thickness should be at least 3 cm for strength. Hollow blocks are popular in Africa because they save money. Interlocking blocks have a tongue-and-groove shape so they fit together without mortar. They are faster to build and stronger in earthquake zones. But they require a precise mould, usually metal, and a strong mix (1:5 cement to sand). You can buy interlocking moulds for $100â$300. They are common in East Africa (e.g., the

or ISSB). You can also make solid blocks with a decorative faceâjust add a metal plate with a pattern to the mould. For all special blocks, the mix must be consistent. Use a measuring box (a 20-litre bucket) for cement and sand. Do not guess. Curing is critical: hollow and interlocking blocks need 14 days of curing because they have less mass. Water them twice a day. Test each batch: break one block after 7 days. If it breaks easily, increase cement. In Africa, many artisans make hollow blocks with a simple wooden core. Start with one type, perfect it, then expand. Remember: special blocks sell for 20â50% more than solid blocks, so they are worth learning.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Making Blocks Step-by-Step

In African block yards, the difference between profit and loss is often decided in the last 30 seconds before a block leaves its mould. A well-filled, properly compacted block with clean corners can be stacked immediately and sold within days. A block with a cracked corner, a weak shoulder, or a honeycombed face is a write-off â wasted cement, wasted sand, wasted labour, and lost customer trust. This practical reference gives you the field-tested steps, numbers, and checks that keep your production line profitable.

Step 1: Setting Up Your Moulds â Wooden vs. Metal

Your mould choice determines your production speed, block tolerance, and maintenance cost. Wooden moulds are cheap to make locally (often from mahogany, iroko, or eucalyptus planks) and can be repaired by any village carpenter. But timber swells in the rains, shrinks in the dry season, and wears quickly â especially when you compact with a manual machine. Metal moulds (mild steel or galvanised sheet) hold their dimensions through thousands of cycles, give sharper corners, and produce blocks that stack more accurately. The trade-off is higher upfront cost and the need for a welder when they dent.

Business rule of thumb: If you produce fewer than 200 blocks per day, wooden moulds may be adequate. Above 300 blocks per day, metal moulds pay for themselves within 2â3 months through reduced breakage and faster demoulding.

Step 2: Preparing the Mould â Oiling and Cleaning

Every mould must be cleaned after each demould. Leftover mortar sets like stone and will scratch your next block. Use a wire brush and a wooden scraper â never a hammer, which dents metal and splits timber. Then apply a thin film of release oil: used engine oil, vegetable oil, or commercial mould oil. Too much oil stains the block and weakens the face; too little and the corners tear. A light brush coat is enough.

Step 3: Filling and Compacting the Mix

Do not dump the whole mix in at once. Fill in three layers, compacting each layer with a tamper or machine. Aim for a mix that holds its shape when squeezed but does not bleed water. A common African yard mix is 1 part cement : 6 parts sand : 4 parts coarse aggregate (or 1:5:5 for hollow blocks). Water should be added gradually â target a slump of 0â25 mm for machine compaction, 25â50 mm for hand tamping.

Table 1: Typical block mix ratios and expected strengths (Africa context)
Block type Cement : Sand : Aggregate Water/cement ratio 28-day compressive strength (MPa) Typical use
Solid load-bearing 1 : 4 : 4 0.45â0.50 7.0â10.0 Foundation, columns
Hollow load-bearing 1 : 5 : 5 0.45â0.50 5.0â7.0 Walls, 2-storey
Hollow non-load-bearing 1 : 6 : 6 0.50â0.55 3.5â5.0 Partition walls
Interlocking (dry-stack) 1 : 5 : 5 0.40â0.45 7.0â9.0 Low-cost housing

Source: Adapted from Kenya Bureau of Standards, KS 1802:2016 â Concrete masonry units, and Tanzania Bureau of Standards, TZS 283:2014.

Step 4: Manual Machine vs. Hand Tamping

A manual block-making machine (lever-operated or vibrating) applies consistent pressure across the whole mould, producing denser, stronger blocks with fewer voids. Hand tamping with a wooden or steel tamper is cheaper but relies entirely on operator skill â and operators get tired. In a business, consistency sells. If you are supplying a contractor or a hardware shop, invest in a manual machine. If you are building your own house on weekends, hand tamping is acceptable.

Table 2: Manual machine vs. hand tamping â business comparison
Factor Manual block machine Hand tamping
Output per day (2 workers) 400â800 blocks 150â300 blocks
Block density consistency High Variable
Breakage rate at demould 2â5% 8â15%
Upfront cost (USD) 300â1,200 10â50
Payback period 2â4 months N/A
Best for Commercial yard Self-build / trial runs

Source: Compiled from Practical Action, Small-scale Concrete Block Production (2020), and field data from Kenyan and Ugandan block yards.

Step 5: Removing Blocks Without Breaking Corners

Timing is everything. Demould too early and the block slumps; too late and it sticks. In warm African conditions (25â35Â°C), blocks can usually be removed after 10â30 minutes with a manual machine, or 30â60 minutes for hand-tamped blocks. Use a flat pallet or board, lift the mould straight up â never twist or rock it. If a corner sticks, tap the mould side gently with a rubber mallet, not a hammer. Place blocks on a level curing bed, covered with plastic or wet burlap, and cure for at least 7 days (28 days for full strength).

â  SAFETY WARNING: Cement dust is highly alkaline and can cause severe skin burns and eye damage. Always wear:
  • Rubber gloves and gumboots when mixing and handling wet mortar.
  • Safety goggles when chipping, brushing, or demoulding.
  • A dust mask when handling dry cement â silica dust causes silicosis.
  • Never add water to a cement burn on skin â flush with clean water and seek medical help immediately.

Step 6: Making Special Blocks â Hollow, Solid, and Interlocking

Solid blocks are the simplest: no core, full fill, high strength. Use them for foundations and columns. Hollow blocks use a core former (metal or timber) inside the mould. They save cement, insulate better, and are lighter to carry â but they demand more careful compaction around the core, or you get weak webs. Interlocking blocks have a shaped profile (tongue-and-groove, or a top/bottom key) that allows dry-stacking with minimal mortar. They are popular in low-cost housing projects in Kenya, Rwanda, and South Africa because they speed up wall construction and reduce cement use by 30â50%. Your mould must be precision-made â even 2 mm of error causes walls to wobble.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Clean and oil the mould before every single block â no exceptions.
  2. Measure cement, sand, and aggregate by volume using the same container every time.
  3. Add water gradually; test by squeezing a handful â it should hold shape without dripping.
  4. Fill in three layers; tamp each layer evenly, especially around hollow cores.
  5. Demould on a flat pallet; lift straight up, never twist.
  6. Stack blocks on a level surface; cover with plastic and cure for 7 days minimum.
  7. Record daily output, breakage rate, and cement used â this is your profit dashboard.
  8. Wear gloves, goggles, and a dust mask â every day, not just when someone is watching.

Further Reading

  • Practical Action â Concrete Block Production (free technical brief)
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards â KS 1802:2016 Concrete masonry units
  • Tanzania Bureau of Standards â TZS 283:2014 Masonry blocks
  • Habitat for Humanity â Interlocking block technology resources
  • ILO â Small-scale construction materials production guides

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. Use these steps as your daily production standard â consistency is what turns a block yard into a business.

quiz.q: Which material is best for a block mould that will be used for thousands of blocks?
quiz.explanation: Metal moulds last longer and keep their shape better than wood.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of oiling a block mould?
options: A) To make the block stronger
B) To prevent the concrete from sticking
quiz.explanation: Oil creates a barrier so the block releases easily without breaking.

quiz.q: How can you test if your concrete mix has the right amount of water?
options: A) It should be runny like soup
B) It should form a ball that holds shape when squeezed
C) It should crumble when squeezed
D) It should drip water when squeezed
quiz.explanation: A stiff mix that holds shape is ideal for strong blocks.

quiz.q: What is the typical cement-to-sand ratio for a solid 6-inch block?
quiz.explanation: A 1:6 mix is standard for solid blocks; 1:5 gives stronger blocks.

quiz.q: How many strokes of a tamper are recommended per layer when hand compacting?
quiz.explanation: About 20â25 strokes per layer removes air pockets effectively.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of a manual block-making machine over hand tamping?
options: B) It produces denser, stronger blocks
D) It works faster in all conditions
quiz.explanation: Machines apply higher pressure, resulting in denser blocks.

quiz.q: How long should you wait before removing a block from the mould?
quiz.explanation: The block should be firm but still soft enough to release easily.

quiz.q: What tool should you use to tap a wooden mould to loosen it?
quiz.explanation: A rubber mallet loosens the mould without damaging the wood.

quiz.q: How much cement can hollow blocks save compared to solid blocks?
quiz.explanation: Hollow blocks use less material because of the voids.

quiz.q: What is a common interlocking block type in East Africa?
quiz.explanation: ISSB and Hydraform are both interlocking block systems used in Africa.

quiz.q: Why is curing important for hollow blocks?
quiz.explanation: Curing allows cement to hydrate and gain strength.

quiz.q: What is the minimum wall thickness for a hollow block?
quiz.explanation: At least 3 cm ensures adequate strength.

quiz.q: How often should you oil a mould when making many blocks?
quiz.explanation: Oiling every 5â10 blocks keeps release easy without excess oil.

quiz.q: What is a sign that your mix is too wet?
options: A) It holds shape when squeezed
B) It drips water when squeezed
quiz.explanation: Excess water weakens the block and causes dripping.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a core in a block mould?
quiz.explanation: Cores create voids, making hollow blocks.

quiz.q: How many blocks per day can a manual machine typically produce?
quiz.explanation: With a team, a manual machine can produce 200â400 blocks daily.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after demoulding a block?
options: A) Move it to direct sun
B) Leave it on a flat pallet in the shade
C) Stack it with other blocks
quiz.explanation: Blocks need to sit undisturbed in the shade for initial set.

quiz.q: What is a good test for block strength after 7 days?
quiz.explanation: A drop test shows if the block shatters or stays intact.

quiz.q: Which oil is cheap but stains blocks dark?
quiz.explanation: Used engine oil works but leaves dark stains.

quiz.q: What is the recommended curing period for solid blocks?
quiz.explanation: Solid blocks need 7 days of watering; hollow blocks need 14.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of interlocking blocks?
quiz.explanation: Interlocking blocks fit together without mortar, speeding construction.

quiz.q: How can you check if a mould is square?
quiz.explanation: Equal diagonals confirm the mould is square.

quiz.q: What happens if you use too much oil on a mould?
quiz.explanation: Excess oil can cause bubbles on the block surface.

quiz.q: What is a simple vibrating table made from?
options: B) A small motor and metal plate
quiz.explanation: A small motor attached to a metal plate creates vibration.

quiz.q: Why should you not use a metal hammer on a wooden mould?
options: B) It dents and damages the wood
C) It makes too much noise
quiz.explanation: Metal hammers can crack or dent wooden moulds.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a simple wooden mould?
quiz.explanation: Wooden moulds are cheaper, costing about $20â$30 in materials.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using a 1:5 mix instead of 1:6?
quiz.explanation: More cement makes the block stronger.

quiz.q: How should you store moulds when not in use?
quiz.explanation: Covering prevents dust and rust.

quiz.q: What is the first step after filling the mould with mix?
quiz.explanation: Compaction removes air pockets and densifies the mix.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good compaction?
quiz.explanation: A smooth, dense surface indicates proper compaction.
